drills.title: vs Monsarichard (795) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You've got pawns on a2 and e2 one square from queening - the game's basically over - but Rg4+ is just a spec check, and it costs you the clean finish. After Kf2, White's king is already sitting next to your e2 pawn; you retreat with Rg5, and Rxe2 mops it up before it ever promotes. a1=Q was simply right: even after Nxa1 grabs the new queen, you tuck the king safe with Kh7 and keep grinding with Rf1, still completely winning. When a pawn is one square from queening and nothing can stop it, queen it first - don't spend the move on anything else.

drills.title: vs Monsarichard (795) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your e2 pawn is one step from queening, and Rf1 does nothing to protect that - so White's knight just jumps Nxe2 and eats it before you ever cash in. You do get some play back with Rd8+ and Nd1+, but it's messier than it needed to be. Rd8 first was cleaner: it puts your other rook on the open d-file, right behind the knight on d4, so after Ra1 you simply play e1=Q+, trade off after Kxe1, and then Rxd4 wins the knight outright - clean and simple instead of scrambling. Get your rooks working on the pieces that are actually hanging before you worry about anything fancy.

drills.coachNote: Look at the diagonal from White's queen on g4 - it runs straight through f5 to e6, so the second you play Qe6 there, Qxe6 just wins your queen outright. Even after Rxe6 trades queens, your bishop on d4 is left completely undefended, and Rxd4 mops that up too - so this isn't just a queen trade, you drop a full extra piece on top of it. c5 was the move: it hits the pawn on b4 and keeps the position balanced, e.g. Bd5 cxb4 axb4 Rxa2 Bxa2 trading down evenly. Before you put a piece on a square, trace every line the opponent's queen already covers - and check what else you're leaving loose.

drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g4 is a sac aimed at White's king on h1 - it's attacked by the queen on g3 and the h3 pawn, so it needs support. h5 does that: if White takes, you recapture with the h-pawn and blow the h-file wide open right next to that king, with f5 and Qg5 keeping the initiative rolling. Bb5 ignores the whole point - it doesn't defend g4 or open a line, so White simply plays Qxg4+, forking your king and pocketing the knight for free. After Kf8 Qh5 you're down a full piece with no attack to show for it. Once you commit to a sacrifice, play the move that actually backs it up.

drills.title: vs Racheeeedgr (827) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: This is a bare queen ending where you're already down 2.8 pawns' worth of trouble, and g6 is just a shrug - it doesn't stop anything and doesn't create anything. White answers Qc4+, you're pushed back with Kh7, and then g4 and Qe5 let White's king and queen coordinate freely while your queen sits doing nothing useful. Qb5 was the active choice: it keeps your queen eyeing checks and central squares, so after Kg2 Kf8 Kf2 Qd7 Qc4 you're still in the fight instead of just watching White improve for free. In a worse queen ending, every move needs to check, threaten, or centralize - passive pawn pushes just hand over a free tempo.

drills.coachNote: Watch the diagonal from White's queen on c5 - it swings straight to f5, hitting both your king on h7 with check and your knight on e4 at the same time. That's exactly what Ne4 walks into: Qf5+ forces Kh8, then Qxe4 just wins the knight outright, wiping out the edge you had. Qe8 keeps your queen safe and flexible on the back rank, ready to meet Qc2+ with Kh8 and trade jabs with Qc4, Qe1, Qc8+ without ever hanging a piece. Before jumping a knight to a central square, check every diagonal the enemy queen can swing onto next move.

drills.coachNote: Your pawn on b4 is sitting completely undefended right in front of Black's rook on c4, and Kf3 wanders off instead of dealing with it - so Black just plays Rxb4 and pockets a free pawn, then keeps the rook active with Ra4 next. Nf3 followed by Nd4 was the move: it centralizes your knight to hit b5 and e6, and even though Black still eventually grabs b4, you get real compensation - g5 forces fxg5 and you scoop up a kingside pawn while your knight dominates the board from d4. In these knight endings, a hanging pawn needs either defense or a bigger threat elsewhere before you spend a move on king shuffling.

drills.title: vs NguyenTuanHai555 (860) — Vienna Game Anderssen Defense
drills.coachNote: Your king on g6 has marched way out into the open, and White's bishop on c4 has a completely clear diagonal through d5-e6 straight to f7, right beside him. Rh8 ignores that, so White plays Bxf7#: check from the bishop, and with the queen on h4 covering the h-file and the knight on g5 blocking his other escape squares, your king simply has nowhere to go — mate, from a position where you'd been winning by over three pawns. Nh5 was the fix: it leads into Qxg4 Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kxg5, trading off the attackers so your king ends up safe instead of mated. When your king has advanced like that, scan every open diagonal pointed at him before playing a quiet move.

drills.coachNote: Bg4 pokes at the queen on f3, but White just slides her to g3 with tempo and you've gained nothing — she's still eyeing g7/h6, while your knight on b8 hasn't even moved. The real issue is White's bishop on c4: it already sits on the a2-g8 diagonal through d5-e6, pinning your f7 pawn to your own king, and that bishop stays dangerous all game — it's the same one that mates you on g6 six moves later. Nc6 was the calm, correct idea, developing a piece and supporting the center before committing the bishop anywhere. Principle: a piece pointed straight at your king like that is a standing threat, not background scenery, until you've blocked or traded it.

Rh1 attacks the queen, but that's irrelevant: Black plays Qxf2#, your king can't take because g3 defends it, and nothing can block in time. drills.coachNote: Black's queen has wandered all the way to g2, and that's a piece you should be hunting, not just nudging. Rg1 attacks her along the g-file, but g2-h3 is still open, so she slides sideways with Qxh3, grabs a free pawn, and escapes — h3 was undefended the moment your rook left h1. Rh2 was the real killer: it comes at her along the second rank instead, and now she has nowhere to go — Qxh2 Nxh2 and you win the queen outright for a rook. When an enemy queen is this deep in your position, map out every escape square before you commit the attacking piece, not just the first one that looks natural.

drills.title: vs Dantempo06 (865) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here with Black's king stuck on e7, and Qg5+ looks natural since it's check — but Black answers Qxg5, you recapture Nxg5, and the queens come off. That's not a disaster, you're still up material, but it hands away the sharpest part of your edge: the mating chances that come from an exposed king with queens still on the board. Qf4 was cleaner — it keeps queens on, and after Qd6 Qg5+ Qf6 Qxd5 you still grab the d5 pawn while keeping real pressure on Black's king. When you're attacking an exposed king, don't offer a queen trade just because it's check — ask whether keeping queens on serves the attack better.

drills.coachNote: Look at Black's king on e7 and queen on c7 — they're one knight-hop apart, and Nd5+ forks both at once. Nxh7 grabs a pawn and you're still crushing, but it lets that fork slip by: Black plays Rd8 and untangles, and while you still win material with Qf6+ and gxf4, it's the long way round. Nd5+ was the knockout — after exd5 you follow with Rfe1+, forcing the king to d6, then Qxf8+ picks off the rook with check too. Before scooping up a loose pawn, scan for a knight move that forks the king with something bigger — that's the move that ends the game fastest.

drills.coachNote: You're up so much material it's basically over, and Qxe5+ is tempting since it's check and wins a pawn — but it lets White block with Ne4, and the game drags on instead of ending. Look at the knight on e6 instead: Nf4+ is check too, and the king has exactly one square, e3, because your pawn on f3 and queen on g3 cover everything else. Once the king lands on e3, Bc5# is mate — your bishop on d5 is already sitting right on that diagonal. The habit to build: when you're this far ahead and more than one check is on the board, compare them before playing the first one you see — the mating check beats the one that just wins a pawn.

That's the gap between a move that just develops and one that develops while stealing material and tempo — Ne6 gets you a similar position eventually, just a pawn lighter and a move slower, which is why the eval slips from +7.8. You were already winning big, so it's not fatal, but the habit is worth building: before playing a normal improving move, check whether a forcing move does the same job and wins something extra.

drills.coachNote: You're already winning big here, so the job is to keep your king safe — d4 ignores that completely. White has Be6+ ready, and after Kh8, Qg6 swings the queen straight at your king with mating ideas around g7; then Be4 lands on the long diagonal, also hitting your bishop on b7, and your huge edge evaporates into defense. Qg5 handles the real problem instead — it meets Be6+ Kh8 f4 with Qg3+ (the f2 pawn just left that diagonal), forcing Qf2 and trading down into a position where you're still comfortably ahead. When you're winning big, spend your move neutralizing the opponent's most active piece, not pushing a pawn.

Qxb7 won a bishop but allowed Qd5 — a queen trade you can't decline (Qxd5 exd5) — and with queens off, the attack on f6 vanished, about five pawns of advantage.

drills.coachNote: Your queen on h7 sees a free bishop on b7 and grabs it — but look at Black's king, stuck out on f6, completely exposed. That's the target, not b7. Qxb7 lets Black play ...Qd5, offering a trade that also kicks your knight: after ...Qxd5, exd5, your knight on c4 gets shoved back to d2 by that very pawn, and your crushing +8.4 collapses to about +3 because you traded off your attacker for a pawn. Ne5 was the move — it keeps hunting the king, and after ...Qg8, Nd7+, ...Kg5, h4+ you're dragging that king across the board. When the enemy king's this exposed, chase it before you go shopping for pawns.

drills.explanation: Ne5 puts the knight on a square the d4 pawn protects and attacks the knight on g6. If Nxe5, dxe5+ regains the piece with check, and after Qxe5 your Qf3+ keeps queens on against his airy king. Your Qf3+ instead offered the trade Black wanted: Qxf3 gxf3 killed all the pressure, and Nf4 came next, poking at the h3 pawn.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Same game, a few moves on — Black's king is still stuck on f6, but a check isn't automatically good if it just invites a trade. Qf3+ gets met by ...Qxf3, ...gxf3 recaptures, and now the knight you needed for the attack gets answered by Black's knight jumping to f4, turning your crushing attack into a slow grind — +8 down to about +5.3. Ne5 first was the key: offer the knight trade, and if ...Nxe5, dxe5+ is check since the king's on f6, forcing the queen to recapture on e5 — only then does Qf3+ actually bite, driving the king to g7. Order matters: set up the check that can't just be traded off.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Look at what's defending your rook on e8 — it's your rook on f8, and nothing else. Rxf4 pulls that very rook away to grab the knight, so the instant it moves, White's queen on h5 has a clean diagonal — h5, g6, f7, e8 — straight onto your now-undefended rook: Qxe8+ wins it outright, and after ...Kh7, Qe6 you're getting steamrolled, a full six-pawn swing. Qxf4 was the move instead — same knight, same square, but your queen takes it while the rook stays home guarding e8, so you keep the material and the position holds. Before you grab something, ask what else that piece was protecting.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Take a look at your knight on c4 — nobody's covering it, and White's queen on d1 has a clean diagonal to e2, from where it lands right on that knight. Castling with O-O ignores that completely: Qe2 comes with tempo, and while you scramble for counterplay with ...c6, White just takes with bxc6 and pushes ...b5 while your knight sits exposed. a6 was the move that actually deals with it — it hits the b5 pawn first, so after bxa6, ...Rxa6 your rook lands active on the a-file with real purpose, and you're setting the agenda instead of reacting to Qe2. Before tucking your king away, check whether one of your pieces is about to get hit.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps to g4 — but who's covering that square? Nobody. White's queen sits on d1, and d1-e2-f3-g4 is a wide-open diagonal straight to it, so Qxg4 just wins the piece for nothing, no trade, no compensation — that's your entire 4.5-pawn swing in one move. After Qxg4, White's simply up a knight and mops up with ...e5, Qg3, Re8. c5 was the simple, correct idea instead — grab queenside space, and after Re1, ...Nc6, b4, ...b6, Bb2 you're developing naturally with everyone defended. This is the one to hammer home: before any piece lands on a square, scan every line pointing at it, especially the queen's diagonals.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Right before this move, look at the diagonal running from a2 through your own bishop on e6 to f7 and your king on g8 — White's bishop on a2 sits there completely undefended... well, defended only by the rook, meaning Bxa2 just wins it outright for you since Rxa2 is forced. Instead Rad8 let that bishop live, and now Bh6 hits g7, forcing g6 and cracking your king's shelter, then Bxe6 fxe6 trades off your good bishop and wrecks your pawns. You were up over four pawns — that's the kind of free capture you take immediately, not the kind you postpone for a developing move.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at c6 and then d8 — your knight on c5 can take the knight on c6, and because that knight was the only guard of d8, the follow-up Nxd8 forks in and wins material outright, with Qxg5 mopping up a pawn on top. That's the whole point of Nxc6: it's not just a trade, it's the first move of a combination that keeps White clearly winning. a4 ignores all of that and just pushes a queenside pawn, letting Black play Nxe5, trade down, and land a knight on e4 that erases most of your edge. When a capture opens a fork on an undefended back-rank square like d8, that beats any positional pawn move.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: The same shot from last move was still on the board — Nxc6 first, and after bxc6 you follow with Qd3 hitting Black's loose pieces and keep grinding out material with Nxc5. b5 walked right past it again, and this time Black punished you with Nxe5, snapping off a knight, then jumping ...Nb3 to fork your rook on a1, bleeding away more of your advantage. Two moves in a row you had a clean capture on c6 that stayed winning several moves deep — the takeaway is to check forcing captures on the board before reaching for a pawn push, especially when your pieces are this active.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You're up an enormous amount here, so the question isn't 'what's a good move' — it's 'where's the mate.' Rxf7 tears away the pawn shielding Black's king, and after Re2 you finish with Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8#, mate, with your bishop on f6 covering the escape the whole time. Qg5 skips that entirely, and Black hits back with Rxf2, suddenly generating real threats with Qe5 and Rf3 that cost you nearly eighteen points of advantage. When the enemy king has no pawn cover left and you've got this much material, stop looking for a nice square for your queen and start hunting the mating net.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Before you move your queen anywhere, look at c8 — Black's rook there is just hanging, undefended, so Qxc8 wins a full rook on the spot, and from Qb5 you're still completely in control. Qd5 walked past that free rook to grab a central square instead, and Black's queen went on a tear — Qxa3, then even after your Qxd4 grabs a pawn, Qxh3 mops up another, clawing back nearly fifteen points because the hanging rook on c8 never got dealt with. A free rook doesn't disappear if you don't take it, but it also doesn't wait around forever — always scan for hanging pieces before picking a 'nice' square.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Notice the pawns on g5 and h5 are both gunning for your bishop on f4 — that's the real story here, not the check you're about to give with the other bishop. Bf5+ grabs a check, but Black just blocks with e6, and then gxf4 wins your f4 bishop for nothing because you never dealt with what was attacking it. e4 is the engine's fix because it strikes the center right away — even after gxf4, exd5 blows the position open, hits the knight with tempo, and Qa4+ gets you real activity with Black's king still stuck on d7. A check that wins nothing isn't worth a piece hanging elsewhere.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same picture as before — your bishop on f4 is under fire from the g5 pawn — but here the fix is to take the attacker: Nxg5. Yes, Black recaptures with fxg5 and you're trading a knight for two pawns after Bxg5, but with the black king stuck on d7 with no safe home, that's genuine compensation, not a loss. Bf5+ instead repeats the same mistake, sidestepping with check while leaving f4 completely undefended, so gxf4 just hands the piece back for free. When a pawn is actively attacking one of your pieces, deal with that pawn directly before spending a move on an unrelated check.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Look at the diagonal from White's bishop on c1 — it runs straight through d2-e3-f4 to g5, so playing Ng5 walks your own knight right into it. Bxg5 just wins the piece, and it gets worse from there: after f6, White grabs the now-undefended e5 pawn too with Nxe5, so you've lost a knight and your center for one loose bishop capture. Nd6 was the move instead — it pulls the knight to a safe, active square, and even though White still nets the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, you get Be7 and clean development in return, keeping things roughly level. Before sending a piece forward, always check what's already aimed at the square you're landing on.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Notice your knight on g5 — nothing defends it, since your bishop on f5 doesn't actually cover that square (f5-g5 isn't a diagonal). Be7 ignores that completely, so White just grabs it with Bxg5. Worse, that bishop then lands on e7 too, so after Bxe7 Qxe7 you've traded bishops and are still down the knight for nothing — a full piece gone from a position where you were doing fine. The move was Ne6, walking the knight to safety on a solid central square before doing anything else, keeping things equal after Qf3 Qf6. When a piece is hanging, fix that piece first — everything else can wait.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has a clean diagonal to c7, and Black's queen on d8 has nowhere comfortable to hide from it — that's a free tempo sitting on the board. e4 ignores it and just pushes a pawn, giving Black time to play Bd7, tucking the bishop away and quietly solving the problem. By the time you try Bc7 later, the queen just steps to c8 and the bite is gone. Bc7 first would've forced Qd7, then b6 and Nc6 build real queenside pressure with tempo the whole way. When a shot like that is available, grab it before your opponent gets to cover it.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your queen on c2 could jump to c5, hitting Black's queen on b6 along that diagonal and forcing it back to d8. Qc3 skips the threat and just centralizes, so Black gets a free tempo with Bd7, and soon that bishop scoops your pawn on b5 with Bxb5 while your rook has to shuffle back with Rfb1 to hold things together. Compare that with Qc5: after Qd7, Bd6 hits the rook on f8, and once it moves to e8 you win the knight on e7 clean with Bxe7 Rxe7. One queen move creates a threat, the other just parks — always ask which one you're making.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, and the board was screaming Nf5+ — your knight on d6 forks White's king on g3 and the rook on g7 with check in one move. White has to run, Kf4, and then Nxg7 just wins the rook clean, no strings attached. Instead Nb7 sends the knight to a square White's rook can hit with Rc7+; after Kd8 it simply grabs the knight with Rxb7, and the game flips from winning to losing in two moves. When your knight can check the king, always scan what else that same square attacks — here it was a free rook.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were up over six points here, completely winning, and Bxg3+ was right there — your bishop on f4 takes the g3 pawn with check, and after Kxg3 you grab the rook trade yourself with Rxd1, staying way ahead. Instead Rd7 puts your rook onto the same open file as White's rook on d1 with nothing between them, so White just answers Rxd7 and your rook is gone for free. Then bxc6 picks off your knight too, and a totally winning position is suddenly lost. Before parking a rook on an open file, always check whether the enemy rook already sits on it.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You had mate on the board: Qxb7+ from f3 to b7 comes with check, and the king on e7 has no good answer — Qc7 blocks, but Qxc7 is checkmate. Instead exd4 just grabs a pawn and lets Black play Bg7 to start untangling; you're still crushing after dxc5 Qc7 Rd7+, but a forced mate turned into a long grind where Black gets to fight on. When your advantage is that lopsided, the mate is usually sitting right there — before reaching for the obvious capture, take a second to check for a king hunt first.
